messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Claire was seven years old when she learned that safety was a lie. She had been sitting at the top of the stairs, listening to her parents argue, when the sound shifted—from words to something wet and heavy, then a cry. She remembered the way the banister felt under her fingers, the grain of the wood pressing into her palms. She remembered the color of the living room carpet, a burnt orange, and the angle of her father’s shoulders as he raised his hand again. But the moments just after—how she got back to her room, who came to get her, whether anyone said anything—those were gone, a black space that would not yield no matter how hard she pressed.

Thirty-two years later, Claire could still feel her own body on that step: her knees tucked, her back against the wall, her hands clamped around the spindle. When a memory surfaced at an inopportune moment—during a planning commission hearing, or while reviewing a budget line item—her shoulders would lock, her breath would shorten, and she would realize, with a jolt, that she was physically braced, as if she were still that child, waiting for the shouting to stop or the blow to land. It was exhausting, and it was constant.

Her work as a city council member required her to be in many places: community centers, high school auditoriums, the county courthouse, the main municipal building. But over the past two years, Claire had quietly and steadily narrowed the geography of her life. She felt safe, truly safe, only in her husband’s study at home and in her corner office on the third floor—a room she had personally chosen for its single point of entry and its door that locked. Everywhere else invited a low, buzzing vigilance. She watched the hands of strangers in meetings, the angle of a raised arm, the speed of a gesture. She scanned faces for the flicker of anger, for the tightening jaw that preceded a shout. Her colleagues mistook it for attentiveness; they praised her as “thorough” and “engaged.” No one knew she was cataloguing threat.

At night, sleep came in fragments. She would drift off, then jerk awake, her heart pounding, convinced she had heard a crash or a cry from another room. Her husband, Mark, had learned not to reach for her too quickly; a sudden touch in the dark made her flinch. He did not know why, only that something bad had happened a long time ago. Claire had never told him the details. She could not have, even if she wanted to—the gaps in her memory made the story feel incomplete, like a book with pages torn out. She only knew the parts that still lived in her body.

The breaking point came during a zoning meeting in early March. A resident stood up to object to a proposed development, his voice rising, his face red, his fist slamming the podium. The sound—that sharp crack of flesh on wood—sent Claire’s vision tunneling. She felt the banister under her hands, the burnt orange carpet, the sudden silence. She could not speak. She excused herself, walked to the restroom, and stood with her palms flat on the cold sink, trying to remember where she was. When she returned, she voted quickly and left before the next agenda item, ignoring the curious stares.

That night, she told her husband she needed to see someone. She did not say what for. But what frightened her most was not the memory itself—it was the certainty that the danger was still present, that she was still being watched, that she could not tell the difference between a man at a podium and a man in a living room. She hoped a therapist could help her sort the past from the present. She was afraid, however, that the sorting would require her to look at the black spaces in her own mind, and that there might be something in them she did not want to find.
